chapter_summary:
Now that we understand what activities are, let's learn how to move between them. In Android, the primary mechanism for navigating between activities is the `Intent`. An `Intent` is essentially a messaging object that you can use to request an action from another app component. While intents can do many things, like starting services or broadcasting system events, their most common use for beginners is to launch activities.

There are two main types of intents: explicit and implicit. For navigating within your own app, you'll primarily use *explicit intents*. An explicit intent specifies the exact component to be started by providing its fully qualified class name. This is like telling the Android system, "Start *this specific* activity."

To start a new activity using an explicit intent, you first create an `Intent` object, specifying the current context (usually `this` from within an Activity) and the class of the activity you want to start. Then, you call `startActivity()` with this intent.

Let's say you have `MainActivity` and `SecondActivity`. To navigate from `MainActivity` to `SecondActivity` when a button is clicked:

```kotlin
// In MainActivity.kt
import android.content.Intent
import android.os.Bundle
import android.widget.Button
import androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatActivity

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

        val navigateButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.navigate_button)
        navigateButton.setOnClickListener {
            // Create an explicit intent to start SecondActivity
            val intent = Intent(this, SecondActivity::class.java)
            startActivity(intent) // Launch the SecondActivity
        }
    }
}
```

And in your `activity_main.xml`, you'd have a button:

```xml
<!-- In activity_main.xml -->
<Button
    android:id="@+id/navigate_button"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Go to Second Screen"
    app:layout_constraintBottom_toBottomOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent" />
```

When `startActivity(intent)` is called, the Android system finds the `SecondActivity` (because it's declared in the manifest), creates an instance of it, calls its `onCreate()` method, and displays its UI. `MainActivity` then enters the `onPause()` and `onStop()` states, but it remains in the back stack.

What happens when the user presses the device's back button from `SecondActivity`? The `SecondActivity` is popped off the back stack and destroyed, and `MainActivity` resumes from where it left off (its `onRestart()` and `onStart()` methods are called). If you want to prevent the user from returning to the previous activity, or if the previous activity is no longer relevant after navigating away, you can call `finish()` on the current activity *before* starting the new one. For example:

```kotlin
// In MainActivity.kt, if you don't want to return to MainActivity
navigateButton.setOnClickListener {
    val intent = Intent(this, SecondActivity::class.java)
    startActivity(intent)
    finish() // Call finish() on MainActivity so it's removed from the back stack
}
```
Now, if the user presses the back button from `SecondActivity`, they will exit the app (or go to the previous app if your app was launched from another one), because `MainActivity` is no longer in the back stack. Use `finish()` judiciously, as it alters the natural back stack behavior and can sometimes confuse users if not applied logically. A common mistake is using `finish()` unnecessarily, making it impossible for users to navigate back to a previous screen when they expect to.

Another common pitfall is attempting to start an activity that hasn't been declared in the `AndroidManifest.xml`. As discussed in the previous chapter, this will lead to an `ActivityNotFoundException` and crash your app. Always ensure every activity you intend to launch is properly declared. Additionally, ensure the target activity's class name in your `Intent` is correct, including the package if necessary, though `SecondActivity::class.java` usually handles this correctly within the same package.

Implementing basic navigation with intents is a fundamental skill for any Android developer. It forms the backbone of how users move through your application, enabling multi-screen experiences and more complex user flows.

screens.title: Implementing Basic Navigation with Intents
screens.subtitle: How activities talk to each other and how users move through your app

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn the fundamental mechanism Android uses to move between screens: the Intent. An Intent is a messaging object that asks the system to perform an action, and for beginners it most commonly launches another activity within your app. We'll focus on explicit intents, which name the exact activity class to start, and on how startActivity and finish shape the back stack and the user's flow. You'll see concrete code examples for wiring a button to start a second activity, the XML view needed for the button, and how the back button and finish differ in effect. We'll also cover common mistakes that cause crashes, like trying to start an activity not declared in the manifest. By the end of this lesson you will be able to create explicit intents, navigate between two simple activities, and reason about when to call finish to control return behavior. To get hands-on, you will add a button to MainActivity, write the intent code, and verify behavior with and without finish. Keep an eye on the back stack: that idea is what makes multi-screen apps feel predictable to users.

keyIdea.text: Use explicit Intent objects to request the system start a specific Activity, and use startActivity and finish wisely to control the back stack.

narration.text: In the next screens you will gain four concrete skills that make basic navigation dependable. First, you will understand what an Intent is: a message object used to request actions from components. Knowing this helps you choose between internal navigation and system-wide actions. Second, you will create explicit intents to start activities by passing the current context and the target activity class; this is the most common pattern for internal navigation. Third, you will learn to use startActivity to launch a screen and finish to remove the current screen from the back stack, and you'll practice the difference so you can control whether users return. Fourth, you'll handle the device back button and know when to finish or rely on the natural back stack. Each objective includes a small verification milestone so you can confirm competency: run the app, trigger navigation, and observe the stack and back behavior. As you work, note that forgetting to declare an activity in the manifest is a frequent mistake that will crash the app, so checking the manifest is part of verification.

screens.title: What is an Intent?
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and a simple analogy

narration.text: An Intent is a messaging object used to request an action from another app component. In practice, beginners use intents mainly to start activities. Think of an Intent as a postal request: it carries an instruction and an address. An explicit intent names the precise destination — the exact activity class — so the system knows where to deliver the message. This is different from implicit intents, which describe an action to perform and let the system pick a matching component. A concrete example: when a login screen wants to show a welcome screen, it creates an explicit intent with the current context and the welcome activity class, then calls startActivity to deliver that request. A common misconception is believing an Intent immediately creates a new activity instance on the calling side; instead, startActivity asks the system to create or reuse the target and manages lifecycle changes for the caller. Why this matters: understanding the Intent as a request clarifies when to attach extras (data), when to expect a result, and why the manifest must list activities you might start. To check understanding, imagine two activities in the same package. How would you name the target in an explicit intent so the system delivers the request reliably?

keyIdea.title: Intent defined
keyIdea.text: An Intent is a request object — explicit intents name the component to start and are used for in-app navigation.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is an Intent?
Intent
A messaging object to request actions from other components.
Analogy: an Intent is like a postal request with an address. An explicit intent writes the exact house number (the activity class). An implicit intent describes the task, like "open a map," and the system finds a matching app.
Key point: Explicit intents are the standard pattern for navigating within your app.
Misconception: An Intent by itself does nothing until you call startActivity or a similar dispatcher.
Concrete example
// Create an explicit intent
val intent = Intent(this, SecondActivity::class.java)
startActivity(intent)
Key Takeaway

Intent = request. For in-app navigation use explicit intents and always ensure the target is declared in the manifest.

screens.title: Explicit vs Implicit Intents
screens.subtitle: When to name a target and when to describe an action

narration.text: Intents come in two flavors: explicit and implicit. An explicit intent names the exact component class to start. This is what you use for navigation inside your own app because you know the target activity. An implicit intent describes an action and lets the system pick a component that can handle it, like asking the system to view a web page or share content. For this chapter we emphasize explicit intents. A concrete example: navigating from MainActivity to SecondActivity uses an explicit intent with the class reference. Contrast that with an implicit intent that might open a map app — there you supply an action and data, not a class. A common mistake is trying to use an implicit form when you meant to target your own activity; this can result in unexpected behavior or no matching component. Another error is misnaming the class in an explicit intent or forgetting ::class. java in Kotlin, which leads to compilation errors. The practical rule: for internal navigation, use explicit intents; for cross-app actions that rely on user choice, use implicit intents. Now consider which form matches your goal when you design a flow.

keyIdea.title: Choose intent type
keyIdea.text: Use explicit intents for in-app navigation and implicit intents for system-level or cross-app actions that should be resolved by the platform.

content.html:
Comparison › Explicit vs Implicit Intents
Explicit Intent
Specifies the activity class to start. Best for navigation within your app because it targets a known component.
Example: val intent = Intent(this, SecondActivity::class.java); startActivity(intent)
Common pitfall: forgetting to declare the target activity in AndroidManifest.xml will cause a runtime crash.
Implicit Intent
Specifies an action and optional data; the system chooses an app that can handle it. Use for sharing, opening a map, or sending email.
Example: val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, uri)
Misconception: implicit intents are not for addressing your own activities by class.
When to use
Explicit: internal screens. Implicit: system or third-party actions.
Verification
Run the app and confirm the intended component opens without chooser dialogs unless desired.
Common error
Misused intent types or missing manifest entries cause crashes or no resolution.

screens.title: Create and launch an explicit intent
screens.subtitle: Walkthrough of the Kotlin code to start SecondActivity

narration.text: Let's walk through the canonical Kotlin pattern for starting another activity. Inside your activity class, you create an Intent passing two things: the current context and the target activity class reference. Then call startActivity with that intent. Concretely, inside MainActivity's onCreate, find the button view, set an onClickListener, construct the intent, and call startActivity. This triggers the Android system to instantiate the new activity, call its onCreate, and move the caller through onPause and onStop. A useful tip: in Kotlin the target must be referenced using ::class. java, not just the class name string. A common mistake is to try startActivity with only a class object or to omit ::class. java, which causes a compile-time error. Another error is to call finish too early if you still need the previous activity. The code example shown is exactly what's used in the chapter and has been tested as a simple, reliable pattern. After you try it, observe the lifecycle change and press the back button to see the previous activity resume. Create and launch an explicit intent means intent(this, targetactivity::class.java) followed by startactivity(intent) is the standard in-app navigation pattern.. In practical terms, walkthrough of the kotlin code to start secondactivity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Intent(this, TargetActivity::class.java) followed by startActivity(intent) is the standard in-app navigation pattern.

content.html:
Process Flow › Create and launch an explicit intent
Step-by-step
  1. Create the Intent with the current context and target activity class.
  2. Call startActivity(intent) to request the system open the target.
  3. Optionally call finish() if you want to remove the current activity from the back stack.
  4. Test the back button to confirm behavior.
Pro tip: Use explicit intents for predictable in-app navigation and test both button-driven and device back navigation.
Code example
// In MainActivity.kt
import android.content.Intent
import android.os.Bundle
import android.widget.Button
import androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatActivity

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
  override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

    val navigateButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.navigate_button)
    navigateButton.setOnClickListener {
      // Create an explicit intent to start SecondActivity
      val intent = Intent(this, SecondActivity::class.java)
      startActivity(intent) // Launch the SecondActivity
    }
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Use Intent(this, Target::class.java) then startActivity(intent). Remember ::class.java and manifest declarations.

screens.title: Button and XML wiring
screens.subtitle: Add a button in layout and hook it to the activity

narration.text: To trigger navigation from the UI, add a Button in the activity's layout XML and reference it in Kotlin using findViewById. The layout element simply provides an ID and text; the wiring happens in the activity's onCreate. A short XML example creates a button with a unique id. In Kotlin, you find that view, set an onClickListener, and build the explicit intent to start the next activity. A common beginner mistake is mismatching the ID between XML and code or calling findViewById before setContentView, which returns null and causes a crash. Another common oversight is not using the correct layout file name in setContentView. When you test, tap the button and watch the emulator create the second activity; then press back to validate the stack behavior. This small end-to-end connection between XML and code is where navigation becomes visible to the user, and validating IDs and lifecycle ordering prevents many runtime errors. Button and XML wiring means add a button in xml, call setcontentview, then findviewbyid and set an onclicklistener to create and send an intent.. In practical terms, add a button in layout and hook it to the activity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Wiring UI
keyIdea.text: Add a Button in XML, call setContentView, then findViewById and set an onClickListener to create and send an Intent.

content.html:
Definition › Button and XML wiring
activity_main.xml
<Button
  android:id='@+id/navigate_button'
  android:layout_width='wrap_content'
  android:layout_height='wrap_content'
  android:text='Go to Second Screen' />
Ensure the layout file used in setContentView contains this ID and call findViewById after setContentView.
Common mistakes & fixes
  • Null pointer: called findViewById before setContentView. Fix: move setContentView up.
  • ID mismatch: ensure the XML id matches the Kotlin reference.
  • Wrong layout: verify the correct layout resource is set for the activity.
Check your understanding

Add the button, wire it, and confirm the second screen opens and that no runtime NPE occurs when tapping.

screens.title: What happens when startActivity runs
screens.subtitle: Lifecycle changes and the back stack

narration.text: Calling startActivity triggers the Android system to instantiate the target activity and update lifecycle states for both activities. The system creates the target activity and calls its onCreate, then its onStart and onResume so it becomes visible. Meanwhile the calling activity transitions through onPause and often onStop, but remains on the back stack unless you call finish. The back stack tracks the order of activities so that pressing the device back button pops the current activity and resumes the previous one, calling onRestart and onStart on it. A key point learners miss is that startActivity does not destroy the caller by default; it simply moves it to the background. If you want to remove it, call finish on the caller — but use that carefully because it prevents users from returning. Another nuance: if you explicitly start the previous activity instead of finishing, you may create duplicate instances on the stack. The practical test: open SecondActivity, press back, and watch the caller resume. Ask yourself: do you want the user to return, or should navigation behave like an exit? That decision shapes whether you call finish.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle insight
keyIdea.text: startActivity starts a new activity and pauses the caller; finish removes the caller so the back button won't return to it.

content.html:
Process Flow › What happens when startActivity runs
Back stack behavior

startActivity places the new activity on top of the back stack. The previous activity remains under it and will be resumed when the top is popped.

Lifecycle sequence example when starting SecondActivity:
  • MainActivity: onPause(), onStop()
  • SecondActivity: onCreate(), onStart(), onResume()
  • Press back: SecondActivity is destroyed, MainActivity: onRestart(), onStart()
Design note: Use finish when you intentionally want to remove the previous activity and prevent returning.
Common misconception

Students sometimes think startActivity replaces the caller. It does not destroy the caller unless finish is called.

Key Takeaway

Understand lifecycle transitions and the back stack before deciding to call finish.

screens.title: Using finish() to control return behavior
screens.subtitle: When to remove an activity from the back stack

narration.text: finish() tells the system to destroy the current activity and remove it from the back stack. Use it when returning to the previous screen should not be possible, for example after a one-time setup or a successful login that you don't want the user to revisit with the back button. A typical pattern is to call startActivity for the next screen and then call finish on the caller. But be careful: if you finish too eagerly you can frustrate users who expect to go back. Another option is to explicitly start the previous activity and finish the current one, but that can create duplicate instances unless you manage task flags or launch modes. Concrete example from the chapter: after calling startActivity(intent) you can call finish() on MainActivity so pressing back from SecondActivity exits the app. The common mistake is using finish indiscriminately; always ask whether the previous state should persist. To verify, implement both flows — with and without finish — and observe how the back button behaves. Which user flows in your app justify removing the previous activity? Using finish() to control return behavior means calling finish() removes the activity from the back stack so users cannot return to it with the back button.. In practical terms, when to remove an activity from the back stack. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: finish() behavior
keyIdea.text: Calling finish() removes the activity from the back stack so users cannot return to it with the back button.

content.html:
Definition › Using finish() to control return behavior
Typical code
navigateButton.setOnClickListener {
  val intent = Intent(this, SecondActivity::class.java)
  startActivity(intent)
  finish() // remove MainActivity from back stack
}
Design guidance: call finish when the previous screen should no longer be revisited. Test both flows to confirm the user experience.
Analogy & risks

Analogy: finish is like locking a door behind you. Risk: lock the user out of expected navigation paths if used carelessly.

Pro tip: Only finish when returning provides no meaningful value, such as after a successful one-time setup.
Key Takeaway

Use finish to remove the activity from the back stack, but decide based on expected user navigation and consistency.

screens.title: Back button behavior and returning
screens.subtitle: How the system handles the device back button

narration.text: The device back button pops the current activity off the back stack and resumes the previous one. This default behavior gives users a predictable way to reverse navigation. When you call finish on an activity before starting another, you remove that activity so pressing back from the new screen will not return to it; instead the app exits or the previous app resumes. Another approach is to explicitly start the previous activity, but that can cause duplicate instances. A subtle error students make is assuming pressing back always closes the app; it closes only when no activities remain on the stack. For flows that require a customized back action, you can override onBackPressed or use onBackInvoked in newer APIs to control behavior, but override sparingly — users expect the system back behavior. The practical exercise: add a back-to-main button in SecondActivity that calls finish, run the app, and test both the on-screen button and the hardware back button. Reflect: does your flow feel natural when a user expects to return? Back button behavior and returning means back pops the top activity from the stack. finish removes activities so back cannot return to them.. In practical terms, how the system handles the device back button. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Back button
keyIdea.text: Back pops the top activity from the stack. finish removes activities so back cannot return to them.

content.html:
Core Concept › Back button behavior and returning
What pressing back does
Pop the current activity. If no activities remain, the app exits. If you called finish earlier, the popped activity may not exist and the app behavior changes.
Tip: Prefer default back behavior for consistency; only override when you must change navigation semantics.
Example
// In SecondActivity
val backToMainButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.btn_back_to_main)
backToMainButton.setOnClickListener {
  finish() // returns to MainActivity if it is on the back stack
}
Key Takeaway

Test back behavior with and without finish so user expectations are preserved.

screens.title: Common errors when using intents
screens.subtitle: Manifest declarations, class naming, and call ordering

narration.text: Several predictable errors occur when implementing navigation with intents. The most frequent runtime issue is ActivityNotFoundException, which happens when the system cannot find the target activity. Usually this results from omitting the activity in AndroidManifest. xml or misnaming the class. Another common mistake is calling findViewById before setContentView, which produces a null view and a crash when you use it. Compiler errors can arise from forgetting ::class. java when passing an activity class in Kotlin. Misusing finish can also create confusing back stack behavior if you remove screens users expect to return to. To debug, check logcat for the stack trace, verify the activity's manifest entry, confirm correct package and class names, and ensure setContentView is called before wiring views. Run the app and reproduce the error, then fix one cause at a time. This methodical approach to debugging reduces frustration and helps you learn the lifecycle and manifest system more deeply. Common errors when using intents means when navigation fails, check manifest entries, class names, setcontentview timing, and use logcat to read stack traces.. In practical terms, manifest declarations, class naming, and call ordering. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debugging checklist
keyIdea.text: When navigation fails, check manifest entries, class names, setContentView timing, and use logcat to read stack traces.

content.html:
Comparison › Common errors when using intents
ActivityNotFoundException
Cause: target activity not declared in AndroidManifest.xml or class name mismatch. Fix: add <activity> entry and verify package/class.
findViewById null
Cause: calling findViewById before setContentView or wrong layout. Fix: call setContentView first and verify IDs.
Kotlin class error
Cause: forgetting ::class.java when creating the Intent. Fix: use TargetActivity::class.java.
Debugging tip
Check logcat for the full exception. Reproduce the crash, then fix one suspected cause and re-run.

narration.text: Now put the pieces together in a short practical task. First, open your project's MainActivity layout and add a button with id btn_go_to_second. Next, in MainActivity's onCreate call setContentView for that layout, find the button by id, and add an onClickListener that creates an explicit intent to SecondActivity and calls startActivity. Build and run the app. Tap the button to confirm SecondActivity opens. In SecondActivity add a button with id btn_back_to_main; in its onClickListener call finish to return. Test the device back button in both directions. Then repeat with finish called on MainActivity after startActivity to observe the changed back behavior; now pressing back from SecondActivity should exit the app. Finally, deliberately remove SecondActivity from AndroidManifest. xml and try starting it to observe ActivityNotFoundException, then restore the manifest to see the fix. This sequence helps you understand cause and effect for navigation, lifecycle transitions, and manifest dependencies. After finishing, reflect on when finish made sense and when it did not. narration.text: Let's summarize the essential points to take away. First, an Intent is a messaging object used to request actions from app components; for navigation inside your app, explicit intents name the target activity class. Second, the standard pattern is Intent(this, TargetActivity::class. java) followed by startActivity(intent). Third, finish removes the activity from the back stack so users cannot return to it; use it only when the previous screen should be discarded. Fourth, always declare every activity you plan to start in AndroidManifest. xml to avoid ActivityNotFoundException. Finally, test both on-screen navigation and the device back button to ensure the user flow is consistent and predictable. These checkpoints — intent creation, wiring, manifest validation, and back-stack testing — form a compact checklist you can apply to every small multi-screen feature you build.

What to Remember
Intent
A message object used to request actions; explicit intents target a specific activity.
startActivity()
Requests the system to create or bring forward the named activity.
finish()
Destroys the current activity and removes it from the back stack so it cannot be returned to.
Summary Takeaway

Master explicit intents, verify manifest entries, and test back-stack behavior to create reliable, predictable navigation in your Android app.

Keep these three rules visible as you implement navigation flows, and you'll avoid the most common beginner errors while creating clear, testable user journeys.
